content.text:
The live demo is up at **<https://sw-ml-study.github.io/demo-decision-model/>**, and I verified the deployed page actually runs the model. The more important news is that your read of it is right: it isn't convincing yet, and I now know exactly why.

## Yes, the model is confidently wrong

I ran 96 inputs through the exact Rust model the page uses. The first 60 are the kind of things people type to ELIZA; the other 36 are memes, keyboard noise, and everyday situations. Grading replies by hand (my judgment, so indicative only), **about 45%** of the realistic replies and **58%** of the memes/situations replies were nonsense. **17 of the 27 bad realistic replies came with confidence ≥ 0.85.** The model is sure *and* wrong, which is the worst combination for a project about honest confidence.

There are three causes, and your "none of the other choices" idea addresses the second:

1. **It's misreading the input.** The model hashes words into 1,024 slots, and most words it has never seen land on a slot that a training word already owns. So "I don't know" reaches the model as `robots_are` and `feel_empty`, and it's genuinely confident about *those*. Only 43% of the probe's features are words it ever trained on (27% for the memes).
2. **It has no escape hatch.** Your suggestion is right, with one catch: the escape hatch has to be *trained* on its own examples: off-topic, noise, memes, anything outside scope. An untrained "none of these" option is just another label the model never picks. That's already happening here: FALLBACK exists, but it was trained on small talk about topics, not on "unlike anything I know". The trained version is in the next step, alongside randomly replacing words with an "unknown" token during training so thin evidence gives a flat distribution.
3. **It's trained to saturation.** Loss ended around 1e-6 with no regularization, so nearly everything reads 1.00.

Tuning the confidence on held-out data after training won't fix this. The held-out sentences come from the same frames as training, the model is rightly confident on them, and so the fitted correction stays near neutral. The uncertainty has to be learned from out-of-distribution examples.

## What makes it feel better (prototyped, not shipped)

I prototyped your "earlier you said…" idea. When the model has no real evidence, the page recalls an earlier "my …" statement, the way Weizenbaum's ELIZA did when no keyword matched, or reflects the user's own words back. On a 15-turn conversation:

| You | Now | Prototype |
|---|---|---|
| I don't know | Do you think machines understand people? | Does that have anything to do with the fact that your mom never listens to you? |
| my dog died | Tell me more about your family. | Why do you say your dog died? |
| skill issue | Do you dream often? | You mentioned before that your dog died. Does that still bother you? |

Every reply is still a fixed frame plus the user's own words, so nothing is generated. That changes what the page *says*, though, not what the model *reports*, so it has to land together with the model fix, not instead of it.

## Next: `008-escape-hatch-model`

I've queued this ahead of the literate document, since the demo's quality is the current pain. Say if you'd rather flip them. In order:

- exact vocabulary instead of hashing;
- the trained escape hatch plus unknown-word training;
- the missing intents: "I don't know", questions to ELIZA, thanks, bye, hostility, "always/everyone";
- reflect-and-recall on the page.

Per your note, it compares **10 s, 5 min, and 1 h** training budgets, each in its own process. Each is judged by the probe sets: sensible-reply rate, and how confident the model is when it's wrong. It ships the cheapest budget that reaches the bar. Full evidence is in `docs/experiments/SL01-dialog-probe.md`.

## Two smaller things

- **Chrome extension:** it isn't connected to this session at all. The connected-browser list comes back empty, so it's not about which tab group was used before. Reloading the extension, or checking it's signed in to the same account as Claude Code, should fix it. Until then I'm verifying with headless Chrome.
- **Known gap:** the footer's "literate document" link 404s until step 009 produces the document.

Everything is pushed (`4618fa6`) and the gate passes (30/30 MLPL, 28/28 Rust, 4/4 probes). No blockers.

content.text:
Yes, and it's a good way to show what training buys. My plan:

- **Train once in MLPL, snapshot along the way.** Run a single training run and snapshot the weights at 0 s (random init), 1 s, 5 s and 10 s of wall-clock time.
- **Measure every snapshot the same way:** accuracy, loss, and how confident the model is on out-of-distribution inputs.
- **Scrub through them on the page.** A training slider swaps snapshots and re-runs the whole conversation, so the same inputs visibly go from random to trained.

MLPL stays the only trainer; the page just replays real snapshots. Within one run, Adam's carried state is exactly what we want, so the Q4 trap doesn't apply here.

Before building UI, let me check the premise you're asking me to demonstrate: is each snapshot actually *measurably* better?

Success criterion: on dialogs.txt and dialogs-wild.txt, the nonsensical rate falls sharply AND the model's confidence on its wrong answers falls, measured on an out-of-distribution set, not only validation. content.text:
Yes, the product is the decision model; ELIZA is only the test bench. That changes the timeline plan below. The page's big "ELIZA" title and chat-first layout also get the framing wrong, so I'll fix that as part of this step.

Here's the measurement (one run, snapshotted; 10 s total on this machine):

| Snapshot | Steps | Train loss | Val acc | Wild acc | Confidence (val) | Confidence (out-of-distribution) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 s (random) | 0 | 2.195 | 0.069 | 0.10 | 0.114 | 0.115 |
| 1 s | 11 | 0.021 | 0.845 | **0.80** | 0.562 | **0.564** |
| 2 s | 22 | 5e-5 | **0.879** | 0.75 | 0.815 | 0.771 |
| 5 s | 55 | 1e-6 | 0.879 | 0.75 | 0.864 | 0.835 |
| 10 s | 110 | 1e-6 | 0.879 | 0.75 | 0.866 | 0.837 |

What it shows, honestly:

- **0 → 1 s is dramatic.** The random weights are at chance: 1-in-9 is 0.11, and confidence is flat at 0.11. One second later, validation accuracy is 0.845.
- **1 → 2 s is mixed:** validation goes up 0.035, wild goes down 0.05.
- **After 2 s, accuracy doesn't move at all.** The only thing that keeps growing is confidence, *including on inputs the model knows nothing about* (0.56 → 0.84).

So "10 s measurably better than 5 s" isn't true for this model. It's measurably *more overconfident*, and the 1 s snapshot is arguably the best-behaved of them all.

For a decision-model demo, that's a better story than the one you asked for. What a decision model gets judged on is whether its confidence means something, and this timeline shows accuracy flattening out while confidence keeps climbing. That's the calibration problem, made visible, and it's the case for step 008's escape hatch and early stopping.

So I'm building it that way:

- **The decision model leads the page.** The title becomes "Typed Decision Model", with ELIZA shown as "demo 01".
- **A training timeline with snapshots at 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 s.** I'm adding 2 s, because that's where accuracy peaks. Choosing a snapshot re-runs the whole conversation on those weights.
- **A small chart per snapshot of accuracy against confidence.** It shows the gap opening.

Starting with the export.

first second, accuracy settles at two, and after that training only buys
confidence -- including on 95 unlabelled inputs the model never trained on. The
1 s snapshot is the best behaved on the hand-written set. The sentence under the
chart is computed from the snapshot metrics, not written in advance, and a test
pins the story (accuracy jumps then stops; probe confidence keeps rising) so a
re-export cannot quietly change it.

  tested natively.

  1e-9 at all five snapshots; weights rounded to 1e-4 for size moved no
  probability by more than 5.4e-5 and changed no decision.

decision over 100 repetitions never applied -- cargo fmt had reformatted the
target and a string replace silently matched nothing -- so the live page said
"mean of 100 runs" while timing one run, and its "100.0 us" was a single clock
tick. It now really times 100 runs (about 5 us per decision). Edits in this
session are now checked and fail loudly when their target is missing.

Cost: five snapshots make the page 1.83 MB of WASM, 629 KB gzipped. 653 of the
1,024 embedding rows never change across snapshots, which is the obvious saving
if size matters.

- **It shows training now.** One MLPL run from random weights, snapshotted at 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 s. Pick a snapshot and the whole conversation is re-decided by the model as it was then. At 0 s every class scores about 0.11 and it answers "Please go on." to everything.
- **The decision model leads.** The title is "Typed Decision Model", with ELIZA as "demo 01".
- **It opens with your line:** "The doctor is in. What seems to be your problem?"
- **Links can pick a snapshot.** For example, `?snap=0&say=i+feel+sad` opens on the random model.

## Is each snapshot measurably better? No

| Snapshot | Val accuracy | Wild accuracy | Confidence on inputs it never trained on |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 s, random | 0.069 | 0.10 | 0.115 |
| 1 s | 0.845 | **0.80** | 0.514 |
| 2 s | **0.879** | 0.75 | 0.740 |
| 5 s | 0.879 | 0.75 | 0.808 |
| 10 s | 0.879 | 0.75 | 0.811 |

The model learns almost everything in the first second. After two seconds, extra training only makes it more confident, including on inputs it knows nothing about. The page says so in a caption computed from those numbers, and a test pins the finding so a re-export can't quietly change it. For a model that exists to report how sure it is, that's the central problem, and it's now visible.

## A defect I shipped, now fixed

The live page claimed "mean of 100 runs" for decision timing but actually timed a single run. My edit to add the loop had silently failed to apply. So the "100.0 µs" in your earlier screenshot was one tick of the browser's coarse clock. It now really averages 100 runs, about 5 µs per decision, and I've changed how I make edits so a missed one fails loudly.

## Why "I don't have any problems" still gets a weak reply

This model can only pick one of nine canned-reply buckets, so it has no way to use the user's own words. Real ELIZA would match its `don't` rule and answer **"Don't you really have any problems?"**. Your oracle plan fixes exactly this, so I've queued it (step 010). A faithful ELIZA run over a large, varied set of inputs records which rule fired for each one. The decision model then learns to choose the *move* (which rule, a recall, or "none of these"), and ELIZA's own deterministic reassembly writes the reply from the user's words.

That also removes the bias I flagged earlier, where one person wrote both the training frames and the keyword list. One caution on sources: the repo is public, so I'd use public-domain text (Project Gutenberg first lines, pre-1929 works) plus text we write ourselves, rather than committing large amounts of copyrighted movie and novel quotes.

## Next

The queue is now: **009 publish interim results → 010 ELIZA oracle corpus → 011 escape-hatch model**, then the literate document and training in the browser. Tell me if you want the oracle before the write-up.

For the write-up I need one thing from you: **where will it be posted?** LinkedIn, the blog, and a document for colleagues each call for a different format. The sibling repo did a LinkedIn post plus a PDF.

Everything is pushed (`a10ce04`), and the gate passes: 30/30 MLPL tests, 31/31 Rust tests, 4/4 probes. No blockers.

Why
Store far more model than you execute
FreeToken-style inference wants a model whose experts live on disk, whose hot experts sit in a cache, whose memorized patterns live in a lookup table, and whose depth comes from reusing one block. Each of those is a kind of sparsity, and each can be isolated at microscope scale.

Large models hide these parts. A model of a few thousand parameters can show them, if every intermediate value is recorded and drawn.
moe-microscope
02 / 08   Swipe for what was built →
What
The microscope, not just the model
MicroMoE:
a one-block transformer over a 52-symbol synthetic domain (arithmetic, sequences, MLPL fragments, prose), then four experts behind a router with a load-balance term, then top-2, then true sparse dispatch, then sixteen low-rank delta experts.
Every lesson records itself:
named frames from the training run, annotated what/why/how diagrams, and three measurements: memory, speed, quality.
Written in sw-MLPL
, an array language for ML; twenty language findings met on the way, most fixed upstream the same day.
A live demo
replays the pinned recordings frame by frame in the browser. It is a playback, not a live computation, and it says so.
Rule of the repository: prefer a shipped feature; build from scratch only when watching it work is the lesson, then show both forms with a parity check.

Sparse dispatch
4x
fewer expert row evaluations (13,440 to 3,360) with outputs equal to the bit. And slower in the interpreter: dispatch overhead beats tiny matmuls.

134:#+begin_src mlpl :tangle no :exports both
** A window

Every lesson trains on windows: a prompt, a bar, the answer, and a stop character, encoded by alphabet index and right-padded. The target ~y~ is the input shifted one position, and the mask keeps only the answer and stop positions, so the model is scored on what it must produce and never on the prompt. This block is ~u:domain_window~ written out with builtins; the domain library does the same with a 52-character alphabet whose index 0 is padding. The last line is the value of the final expression, which the interpreter echoes after the printed lines.

#+begin_src mlpl :tangle no :exports both
alphabet = "~ 0123456789+-*=>,[]():abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz_|.";
text = "2+3=|5.";
n = str_len(text);
ids = fill([n], 0);
i = 0;
while lt(i, n) {
  ids = scatter(ids, i, str_find(alphabet, str_slice(text, i, 1)));
  i = i + 1
};
T = 8;
padded = concat(ids, fill([T + 1 - n], 0));
x = reshape(gather_rows(reshape(padded, [T + 1, 1]), range(T)), [T]);
y = reshape(gather_rows(reshape(padded, [T + 1, 1]), range(T) + 1), [T]);
positions = range(T) + 1;
mask = gt(positions, str_find(text, "|")) * lt(positions, n);
print("ids ", ids);
print("x   ", x);
print("y   ", y);

1	
2	Saw #12: A Model That Decides, and an Index That Knows
3	September 20, 2026 • Software Wrighter
4	
5	2655 words • 14 min read • Abstract
6	There is a live demo on the lab bench: a typed decision model --- 33,065 parameters, about 250 KB with its weights, the whole page --- that reads a sentence and returns probabilities over a fixed set of replies, running entirely in the browser on sw-MLPL, with a trace of every decision behind every reply. Jev, TypeSafe's closed System One model, is the inspiration; the open-source response to it is wide; this is the lab's own entry, measured honestly --- including a probe of exactly why its replies sometimes miss. When the primitives prove viable, they land in sw-atlas, an index that knows the corpus, and in the campus tour guide. The facts live in the index. The model holds only the language.tools machine-learning languages projects sharpen-the-saw demo-decision-model typed-decision-model typed-decisions jev typesafe system-one eliza sw-mlpl mlpl calibration wasm rust sw-atlas moe-microscope sw-campus
7	Contents
8	
9	There is a live demo on the lab bench: a trained model — 33,065 parameters, the whole page about 250 KB with its weights included — reads your sentence and returns probabilities over a fixed set of replies, running entirely in the browser, with a trace of every decision behind every reply.
10	
11	Nothing to clone or install: it is at the typed decision lab . This week’s sharpening is that model — why it exists, what it already proves, what it admits it cannot do, and where it goes once it works. The short version of the thesis: decisions, not sentences, are what software actually wants from small models.
12	
13	|
14	
15	| Resource
16	| Link
17	
18	| Typed decision lab
19	| sw-ml-study/demo-decision-model  · live demo  — Choice, Noul and Scale as sw-MLPL primitives; ELIZA as demo 01, every decision traced
20	
21	| Jev
22	| TypeSafe AI  — the System One framing
23	
24	| Builds toward
25	| software-wrighter-lab/sw-atlas  · the plan  · moe-microscope  · the campus
26	
27	| Prior posts
28	| A Tiny Mixture of Experts Microscope  · A Campus for the Public Work
29	
30	| Papers
31	| Persistent Memory  · Simplifying Transformer Blocks  · Sentence-BERT  · SetFit  · Calibration
32	
33	| Comments
34	| Discord
35	
36	A model that does not write
37	
38	Why “Saw”? The name is Habit 7 from Stephen Covey’s The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People : stop cutting long enough to sharpen the blade. This series  is where I routinely add tools and improve the ones I have, on the principle that time spent on the tools comes back many times over in everything built with them. This week it sharpened the smallest tool with the longest reach.
39	
40	The vocabulary is worth learning even if you never build one, because it names a category that gets lost next to chatbots.
41	
42	TypeSafe’s Jev is the inspiration: a System One model, borrowing Kahneman — fast, automatic, non-deliberative. The concrete meaning is that it is non-generative. It does not emit tokens one at a time and hope they parse. It samples a typed decision in parallel against a schema you supply — a Choice from an enumeration, a Score, a Boolean — and returns that with a confidence, in TypeSafe’s published numbers something like 70 to 500 milliseconds, with a footprint measured in megabytes rather than gigabytes. Jev is closed and hosted: a good description of a category, a poor dependency.
43	
44	The lab’s entry is demo-decision-model , a Typed Decision Model built in sw-MLPL , small enough that every parameter, probability, and branch can be printed. Three primitives and one capability: Choice returns a probability per option, the selected id, a confidence, and a margin; Noul returns one probability in [0, 1] for a proposition; Scale returns a distribution over an ordered scale plus its expectation; and Memory — not a primitive — is structured state the program keeps outside the model, which decisions address. All three are specified in the contract; the demo ships the first of them, and Noul and Scale are queued as numbered work behind it, once the thin slice has earned its footing. There is deliberately no fourth primitive, and in particular no:
45	
46	generate(prompt) -> String        <-- not present, and never will be
47	
48	That constraint is the whole point. A generative model asked “which of these is the user asking about?” can answer with a hallucinated option, a paragraph of preamble, or valid JSON describing a thing that does not exist. A model whose output is the schema cannot. The worst it can do is choose the wrong enum value — and if it is calibrated , say so with a low number. Ordinary program code owns every threshold, every side effect, and every string a user ever sees. The model reports belief; the program decides what to do about it.
49	
50	ELIZA is demo 01, and it is a forcing function rather than the point. It is the smallest realistic application that needs all three primitives and memory at once, it comes with a free, exact oracle — the 1966 rules label the training data — and every word it speaks is canned, chosen from a bounded set the program built. The learned model replaces only the machinery that decides which canned response to use. The first slice answers it with Choice alone; Noul, Scale, and memory arrive as the engine deepens, which is exactly why ELIZA was picked. “The model cannot invent an output outside the permitted space” therefore stops being a slogan and becomes something a test can enforce.
51	
52	The open response to Jev
53	
54	Jev is not the only fish in the sea for long. The open-source response to a closed model in a category this attractive arrived quickly, and it is wide — tool-selecting encoders, grammar-constrained decoding, embedded vector stores, graph builders, routers. The table is the short version of the survey; the honest footnote under all of it is that the demo reproduces Jev’s stated contract and calibration objective, not any of these architectures, and depends on none of these projects. Where a number is theirs, it is labelled; everything else is measured on the lab’s bench.
55	
56	|
57	
58	| Project
59	| What it is
60	| What it is to this work
61	
62	| Needle
63	| a 26-million-parameter encoder-decoder for tool selection, MIT, weights and trainer open
64	| the corpus-scale option for ranking resource cards; nothing the 33,065-parameter demo needs
65	
66	| SetFit
67	| few-shot contrastive fine-tuning of a sentence encoder ; retrains on CPU in seconds
68	| the cheapest semantic tier, worth one measurement as a floor
69	
70	| Outlines, SGLang
71	| grammar-constrained decoding; FSMs and CFGs over the logits
72	| for forcing a general model into a schema; a model whose native output is the schema does not need forcing
73	
74	| LanceDB
75	| embedded, serverless vector database in Rust
76	| 300 resources at 384 dimensions and INT8 is 115 KiB; a flat cosine scan beats any index structure at that size and adds no dependency
77

Jev, TypeSafe's closed System One model, is the inspiration; the open-source response to it is wide; this is the lab's own entry, measured honestly --- including a probe of exactly why its replies sometimes miss. When the primitives prove viable, they land in sw-atlas, an index that knows the corpus, and in the campus tour guide. The facts live in the index. The model holds only the language.tools machine-learning languages projects sharpen-the-saw demo-decision-model typed-decision-model typed-decisions jev typesafe system-one eliza sw-mlpl mlpl calibration wasm rust sw-atlas moe-microscope sw-campus
Contents

There is a live demo on the lab bench: a trained model — 33,065 parameters, the whole page about 250 KB with its weights included — reads your sentence and returns probabilities over a fixed set of replies, running entirely in the browser, with a trace of every decision behind every reply.

Nothing to clone or install: it is at the typed decision lab . This week’s sharpening is that model — why it exists, what it already proves, what it admits it cannot do, and where it goes once it works. The short version of the thesis: decisions, not sentences, are what software actually wants from small models.

|

| Resource
| Link

| Typed decision lab
| sw-ml-study/demo-decision-model  · live demo  — Choice, Noul and Scale as sw-MLPL primitives; ELIZA as demo 01, every decision traced

| Jev
| TypeSafe AI  — the System One framing

| Builds toward
| software-wrighter-lab/sw-atlas  · the plan  · moe-microscope  · the campus

| Prior posts
| A Tiny Mixture of Experts Microscope  · A Campus for the Public Work

| Papers
| Persistent Memory  · Simplifying Transformer Blocks  · Sentence-BERT  · SetFit  · Calibration

| Comments
| Discord

A model that does not write

Why “Saw”? The name is Habit 7 from Stephen Covey’s The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People : stop cutting long enough to sharpen the blade. This series  is where I routinely add tools and improve the ones I have, on the principle that time spent on the tools comes back many times over in everything built with them. This week it sharpened the smallest tool with the longest reach.

The vocabulary is worth learning even if you never build one, because it names a category that gets lost next to chatbots.

TypeSafe’s Jev is the inspiration: a System One model, borrowing Kahneman — fast, automatic, non-deliberative. The concrete meaning is that it is non-generative. It does not emit tokens one at a time and hope they parse. It samples a typed decision in parallel against a schema you supply — a Choice from an enumeration, a Score, a Boolean — and returns that with a confidence, in TypeSafe’s published numbers something like 70 to 500 milliseconds, with a footprint measured in megabytes rather than gigabytes. Jev is closed and hosted: a good description of a category, a poor dependency.

The lab’s entry is demo-decision-model , a Typed Decision Model built in sw-MLPL , small enough that every parameter, probability, and branch can be printed. Three primitives and one capability: Choice returns a probability per option, the selected id, a confidence, and a margin; Noul returns one probability in [0, 1] for a proposition; Scale returns a distribution over an ordered scale plus its expectation; and Memory — not a primitive — is structured state the program keeps outside the model, which decisions address. All three are specified in the contract; the demo ships the first of them, and Noul and Scale are queued as numbered work behind it, once the thin slice has earned its footing. There is deliberately no fourth primitive, and in particular no:

generate(prompt) -> String        <-- not present, and never will be

That constraint is the whole point. A generative model asked “which of these is the user asking about?” can answer with a hallucinated option, a paragraph of preamble, or valid JSON describing a thing that does not exist. A model whose output is the schema cannot. The worst it can do is choose the wrong enum value — and if it is calibrated , say so with a low number. Ordinary program code owns every threshold, every side effect, and every string a user ever sees. The model reports belief; the program decides what to do about it.

ELIZA is demo 01, and it is a forcing function rather than the point. It is the smallest realistic application that needs all three primitives and memory at once, it comes with a free, exact oracle — the 1966 rules label the training data — and every word it speaks is canned, chosen from a bounded set the program built. The learned model replaces only the machinery that decides which canned response to use. The first slice answers it with Choice alone; Noul, Scale, and memory arrive as the engine deepens, which is exactly why ELIZA was picked. “The model cannot invent an output outside the permitted space” therefore stops being a slogan and becomes something a test can enforce.

The open response to Jev

Jev is not the only fish in the sea for long. The open-source response to a closed model in a category this attractive arrived quickly, and it is wide — tool-selecting encoders, grammar-constrained decoding, embedded vector stores, graph builders, routers. The table is the short version of the survey; the honest footnote under all of it is that the demo reproduces Jev’s stated contract and calibration objective, not any of these architectures, and depends on none of these projects. Where a number is theirs, it is labelled; everything else is measured on the lab’s bench.

The page speaks only canned strings; the model decides which. Every decision emits a decision-trace-v1 record, and the trace view shows, for every reply, the candidates the model was offered, the probability it gave each, and the one it chose — whose provenance rule is enforced, not hoped for: the answer is one of the offered candidates, or the trace says so. A link can carry the conversation: ?say=my+mom+never+listens+to+me opens the canonical session already answered.

What it measures — and what it admits

|

| Measured
| Value

| Parameters
| 33,065

| Whole demo page, weights included

| ~1.3 ms

| 0.879

| +0.483

Seventeen of the twenty-seven bad realistic replies came back at 0.85 confidence or higher. Where it goes next

sw-atlas first. Somebody asks where that thing about running experts from disk was, and today the honest answer is that I go and look, because I wrote it: a hundred and twenty-four posts, a hundred and thirty-odd repositories, seventy-five videos, a campus that indexes them. Atlas points the same primitives at that corpus — one semantic index over everything the lab publishes, regenerated nightly from sources already maintained by hand, published as a snapshot of hundreds of kilobytes. I've checked the draft against the measured numbers. Most of it holds up, but **seven claims are wrong or out of date as of today's deploy**. Three of those need fixing before it goes out: page size, latency, and "the 1966 rules label the training data". I'm posting this now, before continuing, so you have it in time.

**Needs changing:**

1. **"~250 KB gzipped" (in the abstract, the intro, "Into the browser", and the table).** That was true of the page before today. The live page now carries five training snapshots and is **629 KB gzipped (1.83 MB WASM)**. Either change the number, or tell me to shrink the page. About 650 of the 1,024 embedding rows never change between snapshots, so storing them once should get it roughly back toward 300 KB. That's a guess until measured.
2. **"Latency per decision ~1.3 ms".** That's the sw-MLPL interpreter on the command line. In the browser the Rust/WASM path takes about **5 µs** per decision (averaged over 100 runs). Suggested: "~5 µs in the browser; ~1.3 ms in the sw-MLPL interpreter".
3. **"the 1966 rules label the training data" (the ELIZA paragraph and "The data is free").** Not yet. The 232 training sentences come from templates I wrote, labeled by construction. The "1966-style keyword matcher" is a short keyword list, also mine; it's the yardstick, not the labeler. The real ELIZA oracle is your plan, and it's now step 011. This also qualifies **the +0.483 margin**: the same person wrote both the corpus and the keyword list, and the corpus deliberately includes words the list lacks (mom, dad, anxious, robots, yeah). Suggested framing: "the margin is partly by construction; the ELIZA-oracle corpus is how it will be tested honestly."
4. **"Every decision emits a decision-trace-v1 record."** The schema and its validator exist, but the page doesn't emit traces yet; the trace view is rendered from memory. Suggested: "the trace view shows…; tests enforce that every reply is quoted verbatim from the table it names."
5. **"…writes a row to the results table — or the row is not written."** `train.mlpl` prints its report; I wrote the `SL01` row by hand, with its calibration columns marked as deferred. Suggested: drop that claim, or say "reports against the matcher per class".
6. **"one of the capability probes below exists precisely to check that [models can't be passed into the gradient]."** None of our four probes checks that. It's moe-microscope's finding F7. Suggest dropping the clause.
7. **"1,024 hashed slots — one for each word and word-bigram".** Words *share* slots, and that's the collision problem the post describes later. Suggested: "hashed into 1,024 shared slots".

**Out of date, in your favor:** the training timeline is **live**, not queued. It has snapshots at 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 s, and it shows accuracy settling at 2 s (0.879) while confidence on inputs the model never trained on keeps rising (0.51 → 0.81). That's a strong line for the calibration argument. The "four probes, all green" line is fine as written; if you want more, the fourth caught a trap that had inflated a result from 0.879 to 0.948.

**Checked and correct:** 33,065 parameters with the correct breakdown; val 0.879; the 45% / 58% / 17-of-27 / "I don't know" → COMPUTER 0.86 probe numbers; no-generation; parity tested; `?say=` links; the three primitives and what ships.

**One live defect I'm fixing now:** the demo footer's literate-document link still 404s. Building it next.

        if m:
            out.append(f"*** ~{m.group(1)}({m.group(2)})~\n\n{m.group(3)}\n")
        elif c.startswith("#"):
            out.append("The module comment says what the file is for.\n")
        elif c.startswith("include"):

        else:

        for line in c.split("\n"):

        m = re.match(r'def (u:[a-z_0-9]+)\(([^)]*)\) \{\n  "(.*?)";', c, re.S)
        if m:
            out.append(f"*** ~{m.group(1)}({m.group(2)})~\n\n{m.group(3)}\n")
        elif c.startswith("#"):
            out.append("The module comment says what the file is for.\n")
        elif c.startswith("include"):
            out.append("Its dependencies.\n")
        else:
            out.append("Top-level statements: the script itself.\n")
        for line in c.split("\n"):
            assert not line.startswith("*") and not line.startswith("#+"), (path, line)
        out.append(f"#+begin_src mlpl :tangle ../../{path}\n{c}\n#+end_src\n")
    return "\n".join(out)

- A six-block runnable primer, in order:
  1. A decision is a probability distribution over fixed options.
  2. Confidence and margin are different kinds of doubt.
  3. What a Scale adds.

content.text:
Yes on hashing, but it's only half the problem. The trace splits both symptoms into two causes, and better hashing fixes only one of them.

**1. Hash collisions (about half the false COMPUTERs, most of the false GREETs).** Unseen words land on a slot a training word owns and inherit its meaning: `ok_boomer` reads as `not_trust` (+10.3 toward COMPUTER), `i_hate` as `think_computers`, `dont_know` as `robots_are`, `stupid` as `morning_today` (GREET). Even `computer`, singular, isn't in the vocabulary; it's reading `think_phones`.

**2. Spurious correlations in my training frames (the other half, and not a hashing problem).** Every COMPUTER frame addresses the listener ("are you one of those {}"), so **`you` alone pushes +3.8 to +8.9 toward COMPUTER**. It's in the top three pushes for 9 of the 17 COMPUTER calls: "how are you", "thank you", "what do you mean", "do you dream". Likewise `friend` is one of my GREET fillers, so "my best friend moved away" is a greeting. Perfect hashing would leave both of these intact.

**On hashing specifically:** for this model, hashing has no upside at all. An unseen word's hashed slot carries either nothing (untrained noise) or someone else's meaning (a collision), never its own. An **exact vocabulary plus an UNK token** removes collisions by construction, and the vocabulary is only 459 features. More slots or several hash functions would shrink collisions but still add noise. The only real case for hashing-style features is *character* n-grams (fastText-style), which would let `computer` resemble `computers` and `mom` resemble `mother`. That's a worthwhile follow-up, not the first fix.

So the fix has three parts, and I'll do them in this order:

1. **Testing first:** a labeled evaluation set built from the 96 probes, scored on per-class false-positive rate (especially COMPUTER and GREET) and on confidence when wrong. I'll ratchet it in the gate so it can't regress silently.
2. **Model:** exact vocabulary + UNK, word dropout to UNK during training, and a trained "none of these" class.
3. **Data:** break the spurious cues. `you`, `do` and `are` appear across many classes, fillers like `friend` and `today` appear everywhere, and I'll add the missing intents (questions to the therapist, "I don't know", thanks, bye).

The ELIZA oracle corpus remains the real long-term data fix. I'm moving this work ahead of the write-up, since it's what the demo needs.

## Follow-up: model 2 (`EH01`)

The first three recommended fixes, built and measured against the same probes,
with their labels frozen and committed (`2de9945`) before any new training frame
was written:

- **Collisions:** hashing replaced by an exact 1,173-feature vocabulary; an
  unknown word now contributes nothing, and the page shows it struck through.
- **"None of these":** a trained NONE class with its own examples, word dropout
  to teach that thin evidence is not certainty, label smoothing, and an explicit
  escalation outcome when confidence, margin, or known evidence is too low.
- **Coverage:** seventeen classes, adding DONT_KNOW, QUESTION, ALWAYS, HOSTILE,
  SORRY, CLOSING, WORK and LOSS; frames rewritten so words like *you* and
  *friend* appear across many classes and cannot stand in for one.

| What a visitor sees (96 probes) | v1 model | model 2 |
|---|---|---|
| reply class correct | 40% | **69%** |
| right when not escalating | 38% | **78%** |
| wrong "machines" replies | 12 | **1** |
| wrong greetings | 7 | **0** |
| escalated | 9% | 33% |

On the 78 probes never seen verbatim in training: 62% vs 38%, and confidence
when wrong 0.36 against 0.72. The model now knows when it does not know, which
is what the escalation rule relies on: of 32 escalations, the model's own choice
would have been wrong in 28.

Not fixed: a third of inputs escalate, and in the browser an escalation replies
from the NONE table ("Please go on."), which is safe but flat. Next: reflection
and recall for escalations, a local escalation path to a larger decider over the
same options, and the ELIZA-oracle corpus so the frames, labels and yardstick
stop being one person's.
"""

feat(model2): exact vocabulary, trained escape hatch, escalation -- fewer confident wrong replies

User report: the live demo asked about machines, and greeted, when the visitor
had done neither. Diagnosed with per-feature blame before changing anything:
half from hash collisions (ok_boomer read as not_trust, i_hate as
think_computers, dont_know as robots_are), half from cues in my own training
frames ("you" alone pushed +3.8 to +8.9 toward COMPUTER; "friend" was a GREET
filler). Better hashing fixes only the first half.

Testing first. The 96 dialog probes were hand-labelled into seventeen classes and
committed (2de9945) BEFORE any v2 training frame existed, so the frames could
not be written to mirror the test. score.rs reports what a visitor sees -- the
reply after the policy, escalations counted separately -- and a ratchet test in
the demo crate pins the two complaints so they cannot quietly return.

Model 2 (EH01), with v1 left untouched beside it because SL01 and TL01 are
published and must stay reproducible:
- lib/text: an exact vocabulary (1,173 features) instead of hashing. An unknown
  word contributes nothing rather than someone else's meaning. MLPL has no map
  type, so the vocabulary is a record built through parse_json.
- lib/choice_model: vocabulary featurization, word dropout (two 0.3 copies),
  label smoothing (0.1), and a row-stacking helper because concat is rank-1.
- demos/eliza/v2: seventeen classes -- adding DONT_KNOW, QUESTION, ALWAYS,
  HOSTILE, SORRY, CLOSING, WORK, LOSS, and NONE as a trained escape hatch --
  936 training sentences from frames rewritten so that you, do, are, eliza and
  friend appear across many classes. Several replies are Weizenbaum's own lines.
- tdm-model reads bundle v3 (and still v2), and the responder has a three-way
  outcome: act, none applies, or escalate when confidence, margin or known
  evidence is too low. This is the user's "need more info" outcome: in the
  browser it replies from NONE and says it would escalate; a larger decider
  choosing among the same options is the planned local path.
- The page marks unknown words, shows the outcome, and the timeline shows
  whatever metrics the bundle measured.

Measured on the 96 probes, what a visitor sees (default snapshot 5 min, chosen by
validation 0.884, never by the probes):
                                     model 1   model 2
  reply class correct                  40%       69%
  right when not escalating            38%       78%
  wrong "machines" replies             12         1
  wrong greetings                       7         0
  escalated                             9%       33%
In 28 of the 32 escalations the model's own choice would have been wrong: the
escalation is aimed where it should be. Strict, on the 78 probes never seen
verbatim in training: 62% vs 38%, and confidence when wrong 0.36 vs 0.72.

Training-budget comparison (user direction): 10 s 0.47 probe accuracy, 1 min
0.57, 5 min 0.56, 10 min 0.55; validation peaks at 5 min (0.884) and falls to
0.794 by 10 min, so more time is not buying more. The 1 min snapshot is too
timid in practice (escalates 82%).

Honest limits: a third of inputs escalate to a flat "Please go on." in the
browser; labels, frames and yardstick are still all the author's, which the
ELIZA-oracle corpus exists to fix; the page grew to 865 KB gzipped.

-- the tangle check caught the drift -- and the chart legend and integer metrics
display cleanly.

Gate: `just check` passes clean -- literate PASS, 30/30 MLPL, 38/38 Rust
(including the probe ratchet), 4/4 probes, all nine checks PASS.

content.text:
You can try it now: **<https://sw-ml-study.github.io/demo-decision-model/>** is running model 2 (build `c8269c6`, deploy verified). Force-refresh if your browser still has the old page cached.

## Your two complaints, measured on what a visitor sees

I scored the replies after the confidence policy on the 96 probe inputs, whose labels I froze and committed before writing any new training data:

| | Old model | Model 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Reply is the right kind | 40% | **69%** |
| Right when it doesn't escalate | 38% | **78%** |
| Wrong "machines" replies | 12 | **1** |
| Wrong greetings | 7 | **0** |
| Escalated ("I can't tell") | 9% | 33% |

On just the 78 probes that never appear in training, it's **62% vs 38%**. It's also far less sure when it's wrong: **0.36** confidence on its wrong answers, versus 0.72 before. A test now pins both complaints, so they can't come back unnoticed.

## Why they happened, and what fixed them

I traced both before changing anything:

- **Hash collisions (half the problem).** Words the model had never seen shared a slot with a trained word and inherited its meaning: "ok boomer" read as "not trust", "I hate" as "think computers". The fix is an exact vocabulary, so an unknown word now contributes nothing, and the page shows it struck through.
- **My own training sentences (the other half).** Every "machines" example addressed "you", so any sentence with "you" in it leaned toward machines. And "friend" was one of the greeting words. Better hashing wouldn't have touched this. I rewrote the training sentences so words like these appear across many kinds of reply.

On top of that, model 2 has **17 kinds of reply** instead of 9. The new ones include "I don't know", questions to the doctor, "always/everyone", hostility, apologies, goodbyes, work, and loss. It also has a **trained "none of these" option**, and your **"need more info"** idea as an explicit third outcome: when confidence, margin, or known words are too thin, the program escalates instead of guessing. The escalations land in the right place: in 28 of the 32, the model's own guess would have been wrong.

## Training time

I compared the 10 s, 1 min, 5 min and 10 min snapshots. Validation peaks at 5 min (0.884), which is the snapshot the page uses. 10 min is *worse* (0.794), so more training isn't buying anything here, and the 1-hour run isn't worth doing yet.

## What's still weak

- **A third of inputs escalate,** and in the browser an escalation replies with a flat "Please go on." The next improvement is to have those use ELIZA's "earlier you said…" recall and to reflect the user's own words back.
- **One author still wrote the labels, the training sentences, and the keyword yardstick.** Freezing the labels first limits the bias but doesn't remove it. Your ELIZA-oracle corpus is the real fix.
- **The page grew to 865 KB gzipped,** mostly the five embedded training snapshots.

Everything is pushed, and the gate passes: literate check, 30/30 MLPL, 38/38 Rust including the ratchet, 4/4 probes.

content.text:
You're right, and it's more than tuning. The current page has **no conversation mechanics at all**: no memory, no keyword tracking, no use of the user's own words. So "earlier you said…" can never appear, and nothing in the model can fix that. What made ELIZA feel like ELIZA was the program around the keyword match. Your list is the right design, and it maps directly onto what this repo was built to show: the model answers several small typed questions, and the program owns memory and control.

I'll build it in two deployable pieces, so you can judge the first one quickly.

**Piece 1: program mechanics, no retraining.**

- **Memory, tracked by the program.** Every user statement is stored with its content words (stop words removed).
- **Your repeat rule.** When the user reuses a content word from an earlier turn, reply "Earlier you said your mom never listens to you…", recalling that turn with pronouns reflected. Each memory gets recalled once.
- **Weizenbaum's MEMORY rule** for when nothing fits: recall a stored "my …" statement.
- **ELIZA's decomposition and reassembly,** keyed by the class the model chose. The model decides *which* rule family; deterministic code applies patterns like `* i want *` → "What would it mean to you if you got {2}?", reflecting the user's words back. This is what turns "I don't have any problems" into Weizenbaum's **"Don't you really have any problems?"**
- **The script is data** (patterns, reflections, stop words) in a JSON file the page loads. The later ELIZA oracle can read the same file, and the Rust stays demo-neutral.

**Piece 2: your "multiple questions per input."** I'll add three Noul heads to the model: *is it a question?*, *negative?*, *positive?* All three are answered in the same forward pass as the Choice, which is the plan's "many typed questions against one state". The policy uses them when the Choice escalates, and the trace shows them as bars.

The rule stays intact throughout: every reply is a fixed frame plus the user's own words, reflected. Nothing is generated.

content.text:
It's live at **<https://sw-ml-study.github.io/demo-decision-model/>** (build `aa1bca6`; force-refresh if you still see the old page). It now says "Earlier you said…".

You were right that the model couldn't fix this. The page had **no conversation mechanics at all**: no memory, no keyword tracking, and no use of your own words. So "earlier you said…" could never appear. What made ELIZA feel like ELIZA was the program around the keyword match, and that program is now there.

## Try this sequence

```
I don't have any problems   → Don't you really have any problems?
my mom never listens to me  → Tell me more about your mom.
I want a better job         → What would it mean to you if you got a better job?
skill issue                 → Earlier you said your mom never listens to you.
everyone hates me           → Really, everyone?
my job is killing me        → Earlier you said you want a better job.
```

## What the program now does

The model still only decides what kind of reply fits. Around that:

- **Memory:** it stores each of your statements along with its content words, with common words like "the" and "is" left out.
- **Your repeat rule:** if you reuse a content word from two or more turns back, it brings that statement back with pronouns flipped, as in "Earlier you said you want a better job."
- **Weizenbaum's own memory rule:** when nothing else fits, it brings back an earlier "my …" statement. Each memory is recalled once, and never twice in a row.
- **ELIZA's patterns:** these are keyed to the kind of reply the model chose. For example, "I want X" becomes "What would it mean to you if you got X?", with your words reflected (my → your). Many of the replies are lines from the 1966 DOCTOR script.
- **Keywords can back up a hesitant model:** if the model's best guess is unsure but the input literally contains a matching keyword, the program trusts the two together. So "my boss yelled at me" (the model is only 0.26 sure it's about work) gets "Tell me more about your boss."

Turn the trace on to see how each reply was built: which rule fired, the fixed frame, the words slotted into it, and a memory panel that highlights the statement being recalled. Nothing is generated. Every reply is a fixed frame plus your own words, and a test checks that each reply rebuilds exactly from those parts.

The rules live in a data file, `fixtures/bundles/demo01-script.json`. The later ELIZA oracle can read that same file.

## Not done yet

- **Your other suggestion is next:** asking the model extra yes/no questions on every input: *is it a question? negative? positive?* All three would come from one pass alongside the main decision, and would steer replies when the model is unsure. It's queued as the next step.
- **The model still sometimes mislabels:** "my mom called again last night" gets a recalled memory instead of "Tell me more about your mom", because the model's best guess there is DREAM. More and better training data, especially the ELIZA-oracle corpus, is what fixes that.

Everything is pushed, and all checks pass: 30/30 MLPL tests, 47/47 Rust tests, 4/4 probes.

lines: "Stack two featurized batches row-wise, keeping ids and pooling weights aligned.";

+  "The shared state representation over the caller's global embedding: the mean of the rows the known features address. Every decision head reads this one vector, which is what makes several typed questions cost one pass.";
+  "Logits [N, m] of the caller's global Noul heads cm_N [d, m] and cm_nb [m]: one independent yes-or-no question per column, over the same pooled state as the Choice.";

+  "Label-smoothed Choice cross-entropy plus the mean binary cross-entropy of every Noul column against its 0-or-1 labels ny [N, m]. Composed from log and sigmoid because there is no binary cross-entropy builtin; the small constant keeps the log finite.";
+def u:cm_train_joint(ids, wmask, y, ny, steps, lr, eps) {
+  "Full-batch Adam on the joint Choice-and-Noul loss over all five global params; returns the final plain Choice cross-entropy.";
+    adam(u:cm_joint_loss(ids, wmask, y, ny, eps), [cm_E, cm_W, cm_b, cm_N, cm_nb], lr, 0.9, 0.999, 0.00000001)
+  "Noul probabilities [N, m] from a plain weights record carrying N and nb: the inference half of u:cm_noul_logits, with a sigmoid.";

Model 3 ([`NH01`](catalog/lessons.toml)) asks three yes-or-no questions of every
input -- *is it a question? is it negative? is it positive?* -- from the same
forward pass as the reply Choice: one pooled state, four typed decisions. A
question mark is visible to it now, where the cleaner used to drop it.

Weizenbaum's ELIZA did not answer questions; it turned them back. So a question
is deflected first -- "We were discussing you, not me.", "I ask the questions
here.", "I'm not here to answer questions. What do you think?" -- and never by
echoing it. When the model cannot decide, a longer input is reflected with its
sentiment and a short one brings back a memory.

On the 96 frozen probes the question Noul catches 12 of 13 questions with a 1%
false-alarm rate; the negative Noul catches 66% of negative inputs; the positive
Noul catches only 1 of 5, because positives are rare in both the training data
and the probes. The default snapshot is chosen by validation accuracy over all
four heads, not the Choice alone: the Choice peaks at 2.3 minutes while the
Nouls keep improving to 12, and choosing by the Choice would have shipped a
question detector that missed half the questions. Model 3 escalates 19% of
inputs, against a third for model 2, with the same accuracy when it replies.

the demo never said "earlier you said", never used the visitor's words, and

keyword tracking, recall and ELIZA-style reassembly (driven by

adds question, negative and positive Noul heads that the program uses to
deflect questions and to reflect sentiment.

Noul labels for the probes were frozen and committed (`2beb786`) before any
Noul training annotation existed. Results on the default snapshot: question
0.98 accurate (12 of 13 caught, 1% false alarms), negative 0.79 (66% caught),
positive 0.94 (1 of 5 caught). The positive head is the weak one, and the
reason is data: 76 positive training sentences of 1,000, and 5 positive probes

"""

import re, pathlib, sys
org = pathlib.Path("docs/literate/demo-decision-model.org"); doc = org.read_text()
def section_body(path):
    src = pathlib.Path(path).read_text()
    out = []
    for c in src[:-1].split("\n\n"):
        m = re.match(r'def (u:[a-z_0-9]+)\(([^)]*)\) \{\n  "(.*?)";', c, re.S)
        if m: out.append(f"*** ~{m.group(1)}({m.group(2)})~\n\n{m.group(3)}\n")
        elif c.startswith("#"): out.append("The module comment says what the file is for.\n")
        elif c.startswith("include"): out.append("Its dependencies.\n")
        else: out.append("Top-level statements: the script itself.\n")
        out.append(f"#+begin_src mlpl :tangle ../../{path}\n{c}\n#+end_src\n")
    return "\n".join(out)
path = "lib/choice_model.mlpl"
head = re.search(r"\n\*\* [^\n]*=" + re.escape(path) + r"=\n\n([^\n]+(?:\n[^\n]+)*)\n", doc)
if not head: sys.exit("section not found")
start = head.end(); nxt = doc.find("\n** ", start)
doc = doc[:start] + "\n" + section_body(path) + "\n" + doc[nxt+1:]
doc = doc.replace("A learned vector per slot, a masked mean pool, one linear head.", "A learned vector per slot, a masked mean pool, and heads over that one pooled state: the Choice, and in model 3 three Noul heads trained jointly with it.")
org.write_text(doc)
print("literate section regenerated")

input.command:
cd /Users/mike/github/sw-ml-study/demo-decision-model
just check 2>&1 | grep -E "^(PASS|FAIL)|^Ran|error" | grep -v "tests/test_"
git add lib/ demos/eliza/ crates/ fixtures/bundles/demo01-model3.json fixtures/bundles/demo01-script.json catalog/ docs/ README.md Cargo.lock
git add -A .agentrail/
git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
feat(nouls): several typed questions per input; questions are turned back, not answered

User request: ask the model several questions per input -- is it a question,
is it negative, is it positive -- and use them for control, as ELIZA's program
did. And a note: Weizenbaum's ELIZA would not accept questions; it replied
"I ask the questions", "I'm not here to answer questions", and similar.

Model 3 (NH01) answers four typed questions from one forward pass: the reply
Choice and three Noul heads (question, negative, positive), all reading the same
pooled state -- the plan's one-state-many-decisions claim, now built and
measured. A question mark becomes the word qmark before featurizing, since the
cleaner used to drop it.

Testing first again: Noul labels for the 96 probes were frozen and committed
(2beb786) before any training annotation existed. The corpus gained frame- and
filler-level tags, question marks on some question frames, and positive
sentences, of which it previously had none (76 of 1,000 now).

lib: joint training (label-smoothed Choice cross-entropy plus a binary
cross-entropy composed from log and sigmoid, there being no builtin), a shared
u:cm_pooled, and inference for the Noul heads.

A selection bug found and fixed before shipping: the default snapshot was
chosen by Choice validation accuracy, which peaks at 2.3 min -- where the
question Noul misses half the questions -- while the Nouls keep improving to 12
min. The export now chooses by mean validation accuracy over all four heads
(0.898 at 12 min vs 0.855 at 2.3), never by the probes, and records the
validation Noul accuracies. Snapshot labels now come from the measured clock:
the first run had hard-coded "10 s" for a snapshot that took 21 s.

On the 96 frozen probes, default snapshot:
  question   0.98 accurate, 12 of 13 caught, 1% false alarms
  negative   0.79 accurate, 66% caught
  positive   0.94 accurate, 1 of 5 caught -- the weak head; positives are rare
  replies    71% right after policy, 77% when not escalating,
             escalated 19% (model 2: 33%), wrong COMPUTER 1, wrong GREET 0

Conversation engine: a question is deflected first, whether flagged by the
question Noul or chosen as QUESTION by the Choice, cycling through Weizenbaum's
lines and the user's ("I ask the questions here.", "I'm not here to answer
questions. What do you think?"), and never by echoing the question back. When
the model cannot decide, a longer input is reflected with its sentiment and a
short one brings back a memory -- the moment ELIZA used its memory. The trace
shows the three Noul bars.

Fixed on the way: remembered lines were being cut at "my" ("Earlier you said
your job last week"); only leading fillers are dropped now, and the filler list
is script data.

Tests: Noul parity with MLPL at every snapshot (Choice and Noul, within 1e-9);
ratchets on model 3 (visible wrong COMPUTER <= 1, GREET 0, escalation <= 20%,
>= 75% right when replying, >= 90% of questions caught with <= 3% false alarms);
and a session test for deflection, memory and whole-sentence recall.

Page is 2.8 MB of WASM, 1.0 MB gzipped: three bundles' worth of snapshots is the
obvious thing to trim next.

Gate: `just check` passes clean -- literate PASS, 30/30 MLPL, 51/51 Rust, 4/4
probes, all nine checks PASS.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text:
Model 3 is live at **<https://sw-ml-study.github.io/demo-decision-model/>** (build `5bdd0ad`, deploy verified). Refresh if the old page is cached.

## What's new

- **Several questions per input.** Alongside the reply choice, the model now answers three yes/no questions about every input: *is it a question? negative? positive?* All four answers come from the same single pass, and the trace shows them as bars.
- **Questions get turned back, not answered,** as you described. For example:

```
my mom never listens to me   → Tell me more about your mom.
are you a computer?          → We were discussing you, not me.
what should i do             → I ask the questions here.
why do you ask?              → I'm not here to answer questions. What do you think?
i lost my job last week      → I am sorry to hear about your loss. How are you coping?
skill issue                  → Earlier you said your mom never listens to you.
my job is killing me         → Earlier you said you lost your job last week.
```

It rotates through Weizenbaum's lines and yours, and never repeats the question back as its answer. Question marks now count as evidence (the text cleaner used to throw them away), but "what should i do" is caught without one.

- **Sentiment steers uncertain replies.** When the model can't decide on a longer input, it reflects the input back with its sentiment ("You seem upset that…"). A short input like "skill issue" brings back a memory instead, which is when ELIZA used its memory too.

## Measured on the 96 test inputs

I froze the labels for these yes/no questions before writing any training data, same as last time.

| Question the model answers | Accuracy | Catches the real cases | False alarms |
|---|---|---|---|
| is it a question? | 0.98 | **12 of 13** | 1% |
| is it negative? | 0.79 | 66% | 8% |
| is it positive? | 0.94 | **1 of 5** | 2% |

The replies overall are right 71% of the time, and the model now hands off to "I can't tell" on only **19% of inputs, down from 33%**, with the same accuracy when it does reply. The earlier fixes hold: 1 wrong "machines" reply and 0 wrong greetings, and tests now guard both.

## A bug I caught before shipping

I was choosing which training checkpoint to ship by the main reply decision alone. That peaks at 2.3 minutes, but at that point the question detector **misses half the questions**, which would have broken your deflection rule. The export now picks by validation accuracy across all four answers, which lands on 12 minutes; the test inputs never enter the choice. Checkpoint labels also now come from the measured clock: the first run had called a 21-second checkpoint "10 s".

## What's still weak

- **The positive detector** catches only 1 of 5 positive inputs. "i got promoted today" gets no credit as positive, because positive sentences are rare in both the training data (76 of 1,000) and the test inputs.
- **Words the model has never seen** contribute nothing. So "…i feel awful" doesn't register as negative, because "awful" isn't in its vocabulary. The ELIZA-oracle corpus is the real fix for both.
- **The page is now 1.0 MB gzipped.** Trimming the embedded training checkpoints is the obvious next saving.

Everything is pushed, and all checks pass: 30/30 MLPL tests, 51/51 Rust tests, 4/4 probes.

content.text:
Fixed and live at **<https://sw-ml-study.github.io/demo-decision-model/>** (build `16f5c7b`). "because we did" now gets Weizenbaum's own answer: **"Is that the real reason?"**

**Why it happened:** it's the same flaw as the old "you" → machines problem. The word `because` never appears in the training data, so the model ignored it. The word `did` appears in exactly one training sentence, the question "did you know about…?", so the model learned *did* = question. It scored "because we did" 0.79 on "is this a question?", deflection runs first, and so ELIZA's `because` rule never got a turn.

**The fix:** a question mark is strong evidence, so without one the program now demands more confidence (0.9 instead of 0.5) before treating a sentence as a question. Real questions without a mark still get turned back: "what should i do" scores 0.99, "why do you ask" 1.00, "how are you" 0.96.

**The underlying data problem is not fixed yet.** The training data needs statements that use *did / do / does / because*, so none of those words becomes a cue for one kind of sentence. I've queued that for the next retrain rather than spend a 25-minute retrain on one word.

**Your reports are now permanent tests.** I started `demos/eliza/reported.tsv`. Each failure you find goes in as a line, and a test replays it against the live model on every commit. "because we did" is the first entry.

Everything is pushed, and all checks pass: 30/30 MLPL, 53/53 Rust, 4/4 probes. Keep them coming.

content.text:
This is the largest step so far, so here's the plan before I build.

**The oracle.** A faithful ELIZA: Weizenbaum's DOCTOR script, with keyword ranks, synonym groups (`@family`, `@sad`, `@desire`), pre-substitutions, decomposition/reassembly, `goto`, and the MEMORY rule. It's data run by a pattern engine. For any input it reports *which keyword and which decomposition rule fired*, plus the reply.

**The model learns ELIZA's own decision.** Model 4's Choice is over the oracle's rule ids, not my 17 hand-made classes. Its reply then comes from ELIZA's own reassembly for the rule it picked. That's the research doc's original idea: a learned model replacing ELIZA's matching machinery. It also removes the "one author wrote both sides" bias, because the labels come from Weizenbaum's rules.

**The corpus.** Natural, varied input: dialogue lines extracted from public-domain novels on Project Gutenberg, plus my memes, slang, and everyday lines. It excludes the 96 probes, which stay the test. This fetches a few public-domain text files from gutenberg.org. I'm skipping movie quotes, which are copyrighted, for the public-repo reason we discussed. The earlier `did`/`because` gap should close naturally, since real prose uses those words everywhere.

**Scale.** Thousands of sentences are too slow to featurize in the MLPL interpreter. The oracle tool will featurize in Rust, with the featurizer already parity-checked against MLPL, and MLPL does the training.

I'll do it as two steps: oracle and corpus first, measured on their own, then the retrain.

doc=f"""# OR01: a labelling oracle and a corpus nobody here wrote the labels for

Every earlier model learned labels the author assigned to frames the author
wrote, scored against a keyword list the author wrote. This step replaces that
with Weizenbaum's own decisions.

## The oracle

[`demo01-doctor.json`](../../fixtures/bundles/demo01-doctor.json) is the 1966
DOCTOR script as data: 35 keywords with ranks, 52 decomposition rules, synonym
groups (`@family`, `@sad`, `@desire`, ...), pre- and post-substitution, `goto`
between keywords, and the MEMORY rule. It is reconstructed after the widely
circulated version by Charles Hayden. A demo-neutral engine in
`crates/tdm-model/src/keyword.rs` runs it, and reports for every input **which
rule fired** (`key#i`) and what it said.

It behaves as the published transcript does, and tests pin it:

| Input | Rule | Reply |
|---|---|---|
| Men are all alike. | `alike#0` | In what way? |
| Well, my boyfriend made me come here. | `my#2` | Your boyfriend made you come here? |
| He says I'm depressed much of the time. | `i#1` | I am sorry to hear that you are depressed. |
| I don't have any problems | `i#8` | Don't you really have any problems? |
| because we did | `because#0` | Is that the real reason? |

Two bugs in the first draft of the script were caught by working out the
reassembly numbering before trusting it (a stray wildcard in a `@belief`
pattern, and a pattern on `cant` that pre-substitution to `cannot` made
unreachable).

## The corpus

{len(rows):,} distinct inputs, none equal to one of the 96 frozen probes, split
by a stable hash into {split['train']:,} training and {split['val']:,}
validation:

| Source | Inputs | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| novel dialogue | {src['dialogue']:,} | every quoted sentence of 3 to 18 words from ten public-domain novels on Project Gutenberg (Pride and Prejudice, Alice, Sherlock Holmes, Little Women, Great Expectations, Emma, Dorian Gray, Anne of Green Gables, Dracula, Frankenstein), capped at 700 per book |
| everyday lines | {src['everyday']:,} | slang, memes, workplace jargon and ordinary situations, written for this corpus |
| generated frames | {src['frames']:,} | model 3's template sentences, relabelled by the oracle |

Movie quotes were left out: the repository is public and they are not.

## What ELIZA does with ordinary speech

The oracle used {len(rules)} of its rules. The distribution is its own finding:
**{100*rules['xnone#0']/len(rows):.0f}% of inputs match no keyword at all**
(`xnone`, "I'm not sure I understand you fully."), and the next most common is
`i#11`, the generic "You say ...?". ELIZA was mostly deflecting.

| Rule | Inputs | Share |
|---|---|---|
""" + "".join(f"| `{r}` | {n:,} | {100*n/len(rows):.1f}% |\n" for r,n in rules.most_common(12)) + f"""| ... {len(rules)-12} more | {sum(n for r,n in rules.most_common()[12:]):,} | |

## Found on the way

The novels spell apostrophes curly, and so do iPhones by default. Both
featurizers deleted only the straight one, so "I don’t know" became "i don t
know" and missed every `dont` rule -- on the live demo, for anyone typing on a
phone. Both cleaners now treat `’` and `‘` as apostrophes, with a test.

## Next

Train model 4 to choose the oracle's rule, measure its agreement with the oracle
on validation and on the probes, and let ELIZA's own reassembly write the reply.
"""
pathlib.Path("docs/experiments/OR01-oracle-corpus.md").write_text(doc)
print("doc written")

path="lib/text.mlpl"

# CLAUDE.md — typed-decision-model-foundation

## Baseline expectations for agentrail-driven sessions

You are working with the agentrail saga/steps process. The saga record (the
`.agentrail/` directory) is the durable handoff between sessions — if your
work is not reflected there, the next session cannot see it.

Before reporting work as complete:

- Confirm the active step is reflected in `.agentrail/` and committed.
- Run the project's pre-commit gate (tests, lint, format) before
  `agentrail complete`, not after.
- If you discover unplanned work, prefer `agentrail insert` / `agentrail add`
  over silently doing it inside another step.

## CRITICAL: Agentrail session protocol (follow exactly)

Every session follows this sequence. Do not skip steps, do not reorder.

### 1. START — `agentrail next`
First thing in the session. Read the output carefully: it tells you the
current step number, prompt, skill docs, and past trajectories. If `next`
exits non-zero, the saga is complete or absent — do not invent work.

### 2. BEGIN — `agentrail begin`
Run immediately after reading `next` output. This transitions the step from
Pending to InProgress so the recorded history matches what actually
happened.

### 3. WORK
Do what the step prompt says. Do NOT ask the user "want me to proceed?" or
"shall I start?" — the step prompt IS your instruction. Execute it.

### 4. COMMIT
Commit your code changes with git BEFORE running `agentrail complete`.
The commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at
the moment of `complete`, so the commit must land first.

### 5. COMPLETE — `agentrail complete`
```
agentrail complete --summary "what you accomplished" \
  --reward 1 \
  --actions "tools and approach used"
```
On failure: `--reward -1 --failure-mode "what went wrong"`.
On final step: add `--done`.

### 6. STOP
After `complete`, do NOT make further code changes. Anything after
`complete` is untracked and invisible to the next session. If you see more
work to do, it belongs in the NEXT step, not this one.

## Agentrail metadata discipline

When using agentrail, changes to `.agentrail/` files are first-class project
changes — the same as application source code. They must be committed, and
should be pushed before you hand off.

Before running `agentrail complete`:

1. `git status` — confirm `.agentrail/` files are tracked, not just present.
   Untracked files in `.agentrail/` mean the next session will not see them.
2. Stage and commit source changes and `.agentrail/` metadata together. The
   commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at the
   moment of `agentrail complete`, so the commit must happen *first*.
3. Run `agentrail complete` after the commit lands.
4. Push the branch (or note the unpushed branch state in your handoff).

This is the most common agentrail failure mode: agents do the work, commit
the source, and forget the `.agentrail/` files. The result is a saga whose
recorded history disagrees with git history, which `agentrail audit` will
flag — but only after the damage is done.

### What's hand-editable in `.agentrail/`

Three categories of files live here, and the rules differ:

- **Append-only saga state** — `saga.toml`, `step.toml`, `plan.md`, session
  JSONLs under `sessions/`, trajectory JSONs under `trajectories/`, and
  anything under `.agentrail-archive/`. **Never hand-edit or delete these.**
  They are written by agentrail commands and represent the durable saga
  record; hand-editing desyncs the saga from git history and from prior
  session memory. A direct `rm` on untracked files is unrecoverable.
- **Regenerated state** — `instruction-lock.toml`. Don't hand-edit; it is
  rewritten on every `agentrail instructions apply`, so any local changes
  are overwritten silently.
- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited
  config, like `.gitconfig` or a `package.json`. Hand-edit it freely, or
  use `agentrail instructions profile *` subcommands to mutate via
  commands (which validate field values and surface typos).

## Working a branch in parallel with another agent

If another agent is working this same repo on its own branch at the same
time, you are both writing into `.agentrail/`. Step numbers are
per-branch and *will* collide — you will both have a `003-` — so your
step directories land on identical paths and the merge conflicts. The
**slug** is the only part that can keep the two lanes apart.

Pick a lane prefix naming your slice of the work (`rtx5060`, `rtx3060`,
`api`, `ui`) and namespace your saga with it:

```bash
agentrail rename prefix <lane> --dry-run   # preview, changes nothing
agentrail rename prefix <lane>             # apply
git add -A .agentrail/                     # -A: a dir move is a delete + an add
git commit -m "saga: rename into <lane> lane"
```

`001-setup` becomes `001-<lane>-setup`, and the saga name is prefixed
too. Your directories no longer collide with the other agent's, so both
lanes survive the merge.

**Run it retroactively — that is what it is for.** You do not need to
decide on a lane before starting work. Renaming is not renumbering: step
numbers, statuses, completion timestamps, and recorded commits are all
preserved, so steps you have already completed keep their git-history
linkage and `agentrail audit` still matches them. Unlike `insert` and
`reorder`, which refuse to touch completed steps, `rename` is safe on
work that has already landed.

It is also **idempotent** — steps already carrying the prefix are
skipped — so just re-run it whenever you have added steps.

**Archive your lane before the merge.** Slug prefixing separates the step
directories, but both branches still have a single `saga.toml` and
overlapping step numbers, so merging two *live* lanes still conflicts.
When your lane is done:

```bash
agentrail complete --summary "..." --done
agentrail archive --reason "<lane> lane merged upstream"
```

Because the saga name was prefixed too, the archive directories are
distinct and the merge is completely conflict-free, with both lanes'
histories landing side by side.

Finer-grained forms: `agentrail rename step <N> <new-slug>` renames one
step, `agentrail rename saga <new-name>` renames only the saga.

## Branch handoff after `agentrail complete`

Once a feature branch is committed and `agentrail complete` has run,
signal that it is ready for review/merge by renaming it from
`feat/<slug>` to `pr/<slug>`:

```bash
git branch -m feat/<slug> pr/<slug>
```

The rename is a useful convention regardless of how this project
handles handoff:

- It distinguishes "in-progress work" from "awaiting review" in the
  output of `git branch`.
- Project-specific tooling (CI, release-engineer scans, automated PR
  creation) can key off the `pr/*` prefix.
- It keeps the branch name stable across the review cycle even if the
  feature slug evolves.

What happens after the rename depends on what push capability you
have. See `push-discipline.md` for how to detect capability before
trying.

- **You can push and use GitHub PRs.** Push the renamed branch and
  open the PR:
  ```bash
  git push -u origin pr/<slug>
  gh pr create
  ```
  (Or push and open the PR via the web UI.)
- **You cloned via HTTPS without push access to the upstream remote.**
  Typical when contributing to an open-source project you don't own:
  push the renamed branch to your fork instead, then open the PR
  pointing at upstream. `git remote -v` shows your remotes; add a
  fork remote with `git remote add fork <url>` if needed.
- **Your project has a project-specific handoff flow** (release
  engineer scanning for `pr/*` branches, automated PR creation, CI

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs

tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. Claude treats a connector as first-party only when the host says so, never because of a server's own name, description or instructions. Claude publishes an artifact for apps, sites, dashboards and games, and whenever the person asks for an artifact or an HTML or Markdown file. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. A page declares these through the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of this would make the page more useful, Claude must load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code.** Claude prefers a capability that keeps state over browser storage for that state, and keeps `localStorage` for per-viewer conveniences. Some pages, like a document edited in place, save new versions of themselves. Such a save reaches this session like any other republish, as a notice on a watched artifact or a conflict on Claude's next publish, and Claude then re-reads the page, merges the changes and republishes.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write.
